title: Credit Card Hardship Program: How to Ask (Plus a Phone Script)
meta_description: Behind on card payments after a job loss or medical bills? How a credit card hardship program works, what to ask, a phone script and pitfalls to avoid.
quick_answer: A credit card hardship program is a modified repayment plan some card issuers offer when a job loss, illness or income drop makes payments unaffordable. It may lower your APR, reduce or fix your monthly payment and waive fees. In return, the card is often frozen or closed and your credit report may show the arrangement. Call early, ask for the hardship team and get terms in writing.
key_takeaways: Call before you miss a payment if you can. Ask for the hardship, financial assistance or payment assistance team, because issuers rarely advertise these programs.
Offer one specific monthly amount based on a written budget. Don't agree to a payment you can't keep up, because many plans end after a single missed payment.
Before you agree, ask four questions: Will the card be frozen or closed? How will the account be reported? What will the APR be after the plan ends? What happens if I miss a payment?
Get the terms in writing, or send your own dated summary of the call. Then check every statement and your credit reports against what was agreed.
If you have several cards or your issuer says no, a nonprofit debt management plan may fit better. Walk away from any debt settlement firm that wants fees upfront.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for anyone who has fallen behind on credit card payments, or can see it coming, after a job loss, medical bills, cut hours or another drop in income, and who wants to ask their card issuer for help before things get worse.
intro: Falling behind on a credit card after a layoff, a hospital stay or a pay cut is stressful, and it's natural to want to dodge calls from the bank. But many card issuers have options for customers in exactly this situation. They just rarely advertise them. This guide covers what a credit card hardship program usually offers and the trade-offs to ask about. It also covers what to prepare and gives you a word-for-word phone script and a template for confirming the deal in writing. Finally, it explains what to do if your issuer says no, including nonprofit debt management plans and the warning signs of a bad debt settlement firm. This is general information, not personal financial or legal advice. Programs and protections differ by issuer and country, so confirm the details with your issuer and your local regulator.

steps.name: Work out what you can afford
steps.text: Write down your current take-home income and your essential monthly costs: housing, utilities, food, transport, insurance and medication. What's left, minus a small buffer for surprises, is the most you can offer across all your cards. Pick one specific number for each card, not a range.

steps.name: Gather your documents
steps.text: Before you call, have these in front of you: your account number, your latest statements, your budget, a list of all your debts and proof of hardship. Proof might be a layoff letter, an unemployment benefits notice, a letter confirming reduced hours or medical bills.

steps.name: Call as early as possible
steps.text: Contact your issuer before you miss a payment if you can, or as soon as possible after missing one. Use the number on the back of your card or in your app, and ask for the hardship, financial assistance or payment assistance team. Some issuers also take applications online.

steps.name: Explain what changed and make a specific request
steps.text: Briefly describe the job loss, medical costs or drop in income, and give your old and new monthly income. Say exactly how much you can pay each month. Then ask what programs are available to lower your APR, your payment or your fees.

steps.name: Ask about the trade-offs
steps.text: Ask whether the card will be frozen, have its limit cut or be closed. Also ask how the account will be reported to the credit bureaus, how long the plan lasts, what your APR will be afterwards and what happens if you miss a plan payment.

steps.name: Only accept a plan you can keep up with
steps.text: If the payment on offer is too high, say so and ask for a lower option. You can also ask how long the offer stays open and take time to review it. A plan you can't sustain can leave you worse off than before.

steps.name: Get the terms in writing
steps.text: Ask for the agreement by email, secure message, mail or through your online account. Note the representative's name or ID and a reference number. If the issuer won't send written terms, send your own dated summary of what was agreed and keep a copy.

steps.name: Set up payments and monitor your accounts
steps.text: Set up reminders or autopay for the new plan amount. Cancel or update any old autopay so you don't pay twice or overdraw your bank account. Check each statement against the agreed terms, and review your credit reports a month or two later.

steps.name: Escalate or explore alternatives if needed
steps.text: If you're turned down or the plan isn't enough, ask for a supervisor or call back another day. You can also book a free session with a reputable nonprofit credit counselor to talk through a debt management plan and your other options.

sections.heading: What a credit card hardship program usually offers
paragraphs: A credit card hardship program is a changed repayment arrangement that a card issuer may agree to when you can't keep up with normal payments. Common reasons include a job loss, illness, medical bills, divorce, a disaster or another drop in income. Issuers call it different things, such as financial hardship program, payment assistance, forbearance or workout program. Many don't advertise it, so you usually have to ask.

In the US, card issuers generally aren't required to offer hardship help. Each issuer decides who qualifies and on what terms, and the terms vary widely. Some countries, such as the UK and Australia, have rules that require lenders to consider hardship requests. If you live outside the US, check your financial regulator's website to see what applies to you.

Most plans fall into two broad types. Short-term plans are meant to get you through a temporary setback and usually last a set number of months. Longer-term workout plans set a fixed payment designed to clear the balance over a longer period, and they often require the account to be closed. Ask which type you're being offered. Common features are listed below, though no program is guaranteed to include all of them.
bullets: A temporarily lower APR (annual percentage rate) while the program lasts.
A lower minimum payment, or a fixed monthly payment for a set number of months.
Late fees or other penalty fees waived, and sometimes a refund of recent fees.
Occasionally, a short pause in payments. Ask whether interest keeps building during the pause.
A way to bring a past-due account back to current status after a run of on-time plan payments, sometimes called re-aging. Ask whether this applies to you.

sections.heading: The trade-offs to ask about before you agree
paragraphs: The main costs of a hardship program are losing use of the card and possible effects on your credit report, so ask about both before you accept. Many issuers freeze the card, cut the credit limit or close the account during the program. Some won't reopen it afterwards.

A frozen or closed card can raise your credit utilization ratio, which is the share of your total card limits that you're using. A higher ratio can lower your credit scores. The issuer may also add a comment to your credit report showing a hardship or modified payment arrangement, so ask exactly what will be reported.

Late payments that have already been reported generally stay on your record. In the US, they can stay for up to seven years. A hardship plan won't erase them, but it can stop new ones from building up. For many people, a frozen card is a better outcome than months of missed payments, collections and a charge-off, where the issuer writes the debt off as a loss but you still owe it.
bullets: Will my card be frozen, have its limit cut or be closed? Can it be reopened later?
How will the account be reported to the credit bureaus during and after the program?
If I'm already behind, will on-time plan payments bring the account back to current?
What is my APR during the program, and what will it be when the program ends?
What happens if I miss a plan payment? Do the original rate and fees come back?
Will fees already charged be waived or refunded?
Will I lose rewards points? If so, redeem them before you enroll.
Do I have to pay by autopay to stay in the program?

sections.heading: What to prepare before you call (with a worked example)
paragraphs: Before you call, prepare a simple budget, one specific monthly offer and proof of your hardship. Having these in front of you makes the call shorter and helps you ask for a payment you can actually keep up with. Some issuers approve a plan over the phone, while others ask you to upload, email or mail documents.

Here's an example with made-up numbers. After a layoff, Sam's take-home pay fell from $3,200 to $2,100 a month. Sam's essentials (rent, utilities, food, transport, insurance and medication) come to $1,850, which leaves $250. The minimum payments on Sam's two cards add up to $310, which is more than Sam has. So instead of promising the full minimums, Sam plans to offer $130 on the larger card and $90 on the smaller one, keeping $30 as a buffer for surprises.

If medical bills caused the shortfall, contact the provider as well. Many hospitals and clinics offer payment plans. In the US, nonprofit hospitals are generally required to have a written financial assistance policy, which can reduce bills for patients who qualify. Ask about these options before putting medical charges on a credit card, where they can build up interest.
bullets: Your account number and your latest one or two statements, showing the balance, APR, minimum payment and any past-due amount.
A one-page monthly budget that compares your current take-home income with your essential costs.
A specific monthly amount you can afford on each card: one number, not a range.
Proof of hardship, such as a layoff letter, an unemployment benefits notice, a letter confirming reduced hours, or medical bills and insurance statements.
Recent pay stubs or bank statements that show the change in income. If you're self-employed, a simple month-by-month income summary can do the job.
A list of all your debts, with balances, minimum payments and due dates.
A call log for the date, time, representative's name or ID and reference number of every call. A notebook or a free spreadsheet is enough.

sections.heading: A phone script for asking about a hardship program
paragraphs: A good hardship call does four things: it explains what changed, says what you can pay, asks what the issuer offers and asks for everything in writing. Call the number on the back of your card or in your app, and ask for the hardship, financial assistance or payment assistance team. Adapt the wording below to your situation.

If the offer is more than you can pay, say so plainly: 'That's more than I can manage. Is there a lower-payment option?' If you need time to think, ask how long the offer stays open. If the representative can't help, politely ask for a supervisor or call back another day. Different staff may know about different options.
bullets: Opening: 'Hi, my name is [name], and I'm calling about my account ending in [last four digits]. I've had a financial hardship. I want to keep paying, but I can't afford my current payments. Can you connect me with your hardship or payment assistance team?'
Explain what changed: 'I [lost my job on (date) / have large medical bills / had my hours cut], and my monthly take-home income has dropped from about [amount] to [amount].'
Make a specific request: 'I can realistically pay [amount] a month on this card. What programs do you have that could lower my interest rate, my monthly payment or my fees?'

Ask about the trade-offs: 'How long does the program last? What will my APR and payment be during the program and after it ends? Will my card be frozen or closed? How will this be reported to the credit bureaus? What happens if I miss a plan payment?'
Close the call: 'Please send me the full terms in writing. Can I have your name or ID and a reference number for this call?'

sections.heading: How to get the terms in writing (with a template)
paragraphs: Ask the issuer to send the agreement by email, secure message or mail, or to post it in your online account. Where possible, read it before you make your first plan payment. If you have to make a payment right away to enroll, make it only if the amount matches what you agreed, and ask for written confirmation. The written terms should cover the points below.

If the issuer won't send written terms, make your own dated record by secure message or tracked mail, and keep a copy. You can use this template: 'On [date], I spoke with [name or ID], reference [number], about my account ending in [last four digits]. We agreed to [program name]: a payment of [amount] due on the [day] of each month for [number] months, an APR of [rate] during the program, and [fees waived or refunded]. Please tell me in writing if any of this is incorrect.'

Once the plan starts, check every statement against the agreement. Review your credit reports a month or two later. In the US, free reports are available at AnnualCreditReport.com. Dispute any errors with both the credit bureau and the issuer. If the issuer doesn't fix a problem, US consumers can file a complaint with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). Elsewhere, contact your financial regulator or ombudsman service.
bullets: The program name and its start and end dates.
The APR during the program and afterwards.
The monthly payment, the due date and the number of payments.
Which fees are waived or refunded.
What happens to the card: frozen, limit reduced or closed.
How the account will be reported to the credit bureaus.
What happens if you miss a plan payment.

sections.heading: Alternative: a debt management plan through nonprofit credit counseling
paragraphs: A debt management plan (DMP) is a repayment plan set up by a nonprofit credit counseling agency. It combines several unsecured debts, usually credit cards, into one monthly payment. The agency often negotiates lower interest or waived fees with your creditors, but you still repay the full balance.

A DMP usually starts with a free or low-cost counseling session that looks at your income, expenses and debts. If a DMP fits, you pay the agency each month and the agency pays each creditor. Plans commonly take three to five years, and the cards in the plan are usually closed. Setup and monthly fees vary, are capped by law in some US states and may be reduced if you're in hardship. Get the fees in writing.

A DMP may suit you better than an issuer's hardship program if you're juggling several cards, need more than a few months of relief or have been turned down by an issuer. A hardship program can be simpler if you have one or two cards and expect your income to recover soon.
bullets: In the US, look for agencies that belong to the National Foundation for Credit Counseling (NFCC) or the Financial Counseling Association of America (FCAA). Check for complaints with your state attorney general.
Ask what services the agency offers besides a DMP, what everything costs and whether its counselors are certified.
Be wary of any agency that pushes a DMP before reviewing your budget or pressures you to sign quickly. Nonprofit status alone doesn't guarantee low fees or good advice.

Outside the US, free debt advice is available from services such as StepChange, National Debtline and Citizens Advice in the UK, Credit Counselling Canada member agencies and the National Debt Helpline in Australia.

sections.heading: Red flags: debt settlement firms that charge upfront fees
paragraphs: The clearest red flag is a debt settlement firm that wants fees before it has settled any of your debts. These are usually for-profit companies that try to persuade creditors to accept less than you owe. They work very differently from nonprofit credit counseling.

These firms typically tell you to stop paying your creditors and save into a dedicated account until there's enough for a lump-sum offer. While you wait, interest and late fees keep growing, your credit is seriously damaged, accounts can go to collections and creditors may sue. Creditors don't have to agree to settle. In the US, forgiven debt can also count as taxable income, so ask a tax professional how that would apply to you.

In the US, Federal Trade Commission rules generally bar for-profit debt relief companies that sell by phone from charging fees until two things have happened. They must have settled or changed at least one of your debts, and you must have made at least one payment under the new agreement. A request for money upfront is a strong signal to walk away.

If you're already seriously behind, you can ask your issuer directly whether it would accept a settlement, without paying a middleman. Settling still affects your credit and may have tax consequences, so get any settlement offer in writing before you pay.
bullets: Fees charged before any debt is settled.
Guarantees that your debt will disappear or be cut by a set percentage.
Instructions to stop paying your creditors or stop talking to them.
Claims about a 'new government program' that wipes out credit card debt.
Pressure to sign today, or fees that aren't clearly explained in writing.

sections.heading: What to do if you're denied or the plan ends
paragraphs: A 'no' on the first call isn't always final. And a hardship plan on one card won't fix a budget that can't cover the basics, so decide on your next step quickly.

If you're approved, plan for the end of the program too. Put the end date in your calendar, and about a month before it, ask the issuer what your payment and APR will become. If your income hasn't recovered, ask about an extension or a longer-term plan before the current one runs out, not after you've missed a payment.

This article is general information, not personal financial or legal advice. Rules and protections differ by country and state, so check with your local regulator or a licensed professional before making decisions about your situation.
bullets: Call back another day or ask for a supervisor. Ask what would make you eligible and when you can apply again.
Cover essentials first, such as housing, utilities, food, transport to work, insurance and medication, before unsecured debts such as credit cards.
Contact your other lenders as well. Mortgage lenders, landlords, auto and student loan servicers and utility companies may have their own hardship options.
Apply for any income support you may qualify for, such as unemployment benefits.
Book a free session with a reputable nonprofit credit counselor to review all your options at once.

If your debt is far more than you could repay in a reasonable time, talk to a bankruptcy attorney or, outside the US, a licensed insolvency professional. Some offer free or low-cost first consultations.

recommendations.best_for: Readers who want one organized place for their budget, call log (dates, representative IDs and reference numbers), scanned hardship documents and written plan terms across several issuers. Check on Notion's website whether its free plan covers what you need, because plans and pricing change.
recommendations.not_for: Anyone who would have to pay for a new subscription while in financial hardship, or who prefers paper. A notebook or a free spreadsheet does this job just as well. It doesn't give debt advice or contact creditors for you, and you shouldn't store full card numbers or passwords in any notes app.

recommendations.best_for: Self-employed readers and small-business owners who already keep their books in QuickBooks Online and need to show an issuer how their income has fallen. A profit-and-loss report comparing recent months with earlier ones is one example.
recommendations.not_for: Employees who can use a layoff letter or pay stubs as proof, or anyone who would need to start a new paid subscription just to apply for hardship help. Bank statements usually work as proof of income. It doesn't negotiate with creditors or give debt advice.

faq.question: Does a credit card hardship program hurt your credit?
faq.answer: It can, though usually less than continuing to miss payments. The issuer may freeze or close the card, which can raise your credit utilization ratio, and it may add a note about the arrangement to your credit report. Ask exactly how the account will be reported before you agree.

faq.question: Can I join a hardship program if I've already missed payments?
faq.answer: Often, yes. Many issuers consider requests from customers who are already behind, though the options may depend on how late the account is. In the US, issuers generally don't report a payment as late to the credit bureaus until it's at least 30 days past due. Late fees can apply sooner, though, so call as soon as you can.

faq.question: How long do credit card hardship programs last?
faq.answer: It depends on the issuer and the program. Short-term plans usually last a set number of months, while longer workout plans can run for several years with fixed payments. Ask for the exact start and end dates in writing.

faq.question: Will my credit card be closed if I enroll in a hardship program?
faq.answer: It may be. Many issuers freeze the card or close the account during a hardship program, and some won't reopen it later. Ask before you enroll, and plan your budget on the assumption that you won't be able to use that card.

faq.question: What happens when a credit card hardship program ends?
faq.answer: Often the account goes back to its normal terms, which can mean a higher APR and minimum payment than during the plan. Some long-term workout plans instead end with the balance paid off and the account closed. Before you enroll, ask what your rate and payment will be afterwards, and contact the issuer before the end date if you still need help.

faq.question: Is a debt management plan better than a hardship program?
faq.answer: Neither is better in every case. A hardship program can be simpler for a temporary drop in income on one or two cards. A nonprofit debt management plan can combine several cards into one payment over a longer period. A free session with a reputable credit counselor can help you compare.

conclusion: A credit card hardship program can give you breathing room after a job loss, medical bills or a drop in income. It works best when you call early, offer a specific payment you can genuinely keep up with and understand the trade-offs before you agree. Get every term in writing, put the end date in your calendar and check your statements and credit reports. If one issuer's plan isn't enough, or you're juggling several cards, talk to a reputable nonprofit credit counselor before considering any service that charges upfront fees. Terms and protections vary by issuer and country, so confirm the details directly with your card issuer and your local regulator.
